# Italian Pasta Techniques

## Fresh Pasta Dough

Fresh egg pasta is made from 00 flour and egg yolks. Use 100 grams of flour per egg yolk.
Knead the dough until completely smooth, about 10 minutes by hand, then wrap and rest for 30 minutes
to let the gluten relax before rolling. Fresh pasta cooks much faster than dried: typically
two to three minutes in boiling salted water.

## Cooking Pasta

Use a large pot of heavily salted boiling water -- the water should taste like the sea.
Pasta absorbs salt during cooking; under-salted water produces bland noodles.
Cook until just al dente, meaning tender but with a slight resistance when bitten through.
Reserve a cup of the starchy cooking water before draining to adjust sauce consistency.

## Carbonara

Roman carbonara uses guanciale (cured pork cheek), egg yolks, Pecorino Romano cheese, and black
pepper. No cream. Render the guanciale in a pan until crispy. Remove from heat.
Whisk egg yolks with finely grated Pecorino and coarsely ground black pepper.
Add the cooked pasta to the pan off heat, then add the egg mixture and toss vigorously,
adding pasta water gradually to create a glossy emulsified sauce without scrambling the eggs.

## Cacio e Pepe

Cacio e Pepe uses only three ingredients: pasta, Pecorino Romano, and black pepper.
Toast whole peppercorns in a dry pan, crush coarsely, bloom in a small amount of pasta water.
Combine grated Pecorino with pasta water to make a paste. Add pasta, toss with the pepper,
then fold in the cheese paste. Toss aggressively with pasta water as needed.

## Ragù alla Bolognese

True Bolognese is a meat sauce slowly cooked for three to four hours. Brown finely minced beef
and pork in batches until caramelized. Add soffritto of onion, celery, carrot. Add wine
and reduce. Add whole milk and reduce. Add a small amount of tomato paste and stock.
Simmer on the lowest heat, stirring occasionally, until the fat rises and the sauce is thick.
